title: 3D Correlation Space
text:
Asymptotic Distribution
Under standard regularity conditions: normality and finite asypmtotic covariance \(\Psi \in R^{p \times p}\) (and also finite fourth-order moment), CLT shows that \[
  \sqrt{n}(\hat{\rho}-\rho) \xrightarrow{d} N(0,\Psi(\rho))
\]where:

diagonal of \(\Psi\): \(\psi_{jk} = 1-\rho_{jk}^2\)
off-diagonal of \(\Psi\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\psi_{jk,hm}
&= N\,\sigma_{jk,hm} \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \Big[
(\rho_{jh}-\rho_{jk}\rho_{kh})(\rho_{km}-\rho_{kh}\rho_{hm}) \\
&\quad + (\rho_{jm}-\rho_{jk}\rho_{km})(\rho_{kh}-\rho_{kj}\rho_{jh}) \\
&\quad + (\rho_{jh}-\rho_{jm}\rho_{mh})(\rho_{km}-\rho_{kj}\rho_{jm}) \\
&\quad + (\rho_{jm}-\rho_{jk}\rho_{km})(\rho_{kh}-\rho_{km}\rho_{mh})
\Big].
\end{aligned}
\]

When \(\Psi(\rho)\) is unknown, we use plug-in estimate $ \Psi(\hat\rho)$. This requires us to prove \(\hat\Psi \xrightarrow{p} \Psi\).
[See Steiger (1990)]

title: 3D Correlation Space
text:
Confidence Ellipsoid of \(\rho\)
Let \(Z = \Psi^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\sqrt{n}}(\hat{\rho} - \rho)\), we have \(Z \xrightarrow{d} N(0,I_p)\). Therefore, by continuous mapping theorem \(Z^TZ \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{p}\).
The confidence ellipsoid \(C_{1-\alpha} = \{ \rho:  \ n(\hat{\rho} - \rho)^T\Psi^{-1}(\hat{\rho} - \rho)\ \leq \chi^{2}_{p, 1-\alpha} \}\).
All perturbed vectors \(\hat\rho^{\prime}\) satisfying the inequality are accepted as points inside the ellipsoid.
Note: I do think the confidence ellipsoid should be the intersect of \(C_{1-\alpha}\) and the PSD criteria.

Plots:

When \(\rho = 0\) (Identity matrix)
When \(\rho\) is small: correlation coefficients are small; \(R\) is close to the identity matrix; large \(\eta\) value in the lkj-distribution
When \(\rho\) is large (not all \(\rho_{ij}\)s, but some) : correlation coefficients are large; \(R\) is close the boundary of correlation space; extremely small \(\eta\) value in the lkj-distribution

code for epsilon ball.
Sample from a wald-cloud

Sample from the full distributional spread around \(\rho_0\):
Let \(\rho_0 = vech(R_0)\). For testing \(H_0: \rho = \rho_0\), based on asymptotic normality of \(\rho\), we have wald-type statistic
\[
W = (\hat\rho - \rho_0)^T \Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\hat\rho - \rho_0) \sim \chi^2_p
\]
This implies we can draw \(\hat\rho\) under the null distribution \(H_0\):
\[
\hat\rho^{(b)} \sim N_p(\rho_0, \frac{\Psi(\rho_0)}{n})
\]
Or, equivalently, \(\hat\rho^{(b)} = \rho_0 + Lz\), where \(z \sim N(0,I_p)\), \(L= UD^\frac{1}{2}\) (eigen-decomposition of \(\Psi(\rho_0)\).
Sample uniformly around \(\rho_0\):
\[
\hat\rho^{(b)} = \rho_0 + L(\sqrt{c} r^{\frac{1}{p}}u)
\]
where \(c: \chi^2_{p, 1-\alpha}\), \(r\) represent a random radius sample from \(Unif(0,1)\), \(u\) represents the random unit direction, sample from \(N(0,I_p)\) and rescale to have length (norm) 1.
The role of \(c\) is to ensure we sample within some measurable bound (e.g., 95% confidence ellipsoid).
Show code and plots here



Why don’t we use the first approach (Generate data then compute correlation) ?

Making extra assumption: This approach assumes the underlying data distribution, which seems to be unnecessary here in our theory. We only need \(\hat\rho\) to be normal (asymptotically).
To meet out goal as a less expensive approach for resampling. Sample from \(\rho\) directly will be a less expensive approach.

title: 3D Correlation Space
text:
Confidence region of \(\rho\)

Finding Pivot of \(\rho\)
A typical way to construct confidence interval for an unknown parameter is to find its pivot quantity and the corresponding distribution.
From Steiger (1990),
\[
  \sqrt{n}(\hat{\rho}-\rho) \xrightarrow{d} N(0,\Psi(\rho))
\]
Let \(Z = \Psi(\rho)^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\sqrt{n}}(\hat{\rho} - \rho)\), then \(Z \xrightarrow{d} N(0,I_d)\), where \(d\) is the number of correlation coefficients (equivalent to \(\frac{p(p-1)}{2}\) in which \(p\) is the number of variables). We claim that \(Z\) is a pivot quantity for \(\rho\) since distribution of \(Z\) is free from the unknown parameter.
We can essentially use \(Z\) to construct confidence region for \(\rho\).
In the case of \(d=1\) (\(p=2\)),
\[
\begin{gathered}
Z = \frac{\hat{\rho} - \rho}{\sqrt{\Psi{(\rho)}/{n}}} \sim N(0,1)
\\ P(-z_{\alpha/2}\leq \frac{\hat{\rho} - \rho}{\sqrt{\Psi{(\rho)}/{n}}} \leq z_{\alpha/2}) = 1-\alpha
\\ P(\hat{\rho}-z_{\alpha/2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\Psi{(\rho)}}{n}} \leq \ \rho \ \leq \hat{\rho}+z_{\alpha/2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\Psi{(\rho)}}{n}} = 1 - \alpha
\end{gathered}
\]
Note when \(d=1\), \(\Psi(\rho)\) is a scalar, basically variance of \(\rho\). When \(\Psi(\rho)\) is unknown, we can try its plug-in estimate: \(\Psi(\hat{\rho})\).
Some challenges arise when using \(Z\) to construct a confidence region for \(\rho\) in higher dimension:

Because \(Z_i \sim N(0,1)\) for each \(i\) dimension, we are basically constructing confidence interval for each \(Z_i\) marginally. This results in a confidence “box” (or hyper-rectangle) when combined together.
This approach does not respect the covariance of \(\rho\) and treat each \(\rho_{ij}\) as independent. This is incorrect. See Steiger (1990).

This motivates us to consider a joint-inference approach, so that the confidence region that we build respects the covariance of \(\rho\).


Joint Inference on \(\rho\)
By continuous mapping theorem, \(T = \ Z^TZ \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{d}\). Since \(T\)’s distribution is independent of unknown parameters, and that \(T= T(\hat\rho, \rho) = n(\hat{\rho} - \rho)^T\Psi(\rho)^{-1}(\hat{\rho} - \rho)\) is a function of data \(\hat\rho\) and unknown parameter \(\rho\), we can construct confidence region of \(\rho\) using pivot \(T\).
\[
C_{1-\alpha} = \{ \rho:  \ n(\hat{\rho} - \rho)^T\Psi(\rho)^{-1}(\hat{\rho} - \rho)\ \leq \chi^{2}_{d, 1-\alpha} \}
\]
The LHS equation is also known as the Mahalanobis distance/ Wald distance.
Interpretation:

The confidence region (or confidence set) of \(\rho\) is the set of all parameter vectors whose Mahalanobis distance from the observed estimator \(\hat\rho\) is smaller than the \(\chi^2\) threshold.
In other words, the set of all candidate parameter values \(\rho\) that are not too far from the observed estimator \(\hat\rho\) is the confidence region.
The likelihood of the confidence set containing the true \(\rho\) is 95%.

Notes:

The plug-in approach is only true when \(\Psi(\hat\rho) \xrightarrow{p} \Psi(\rho)\).
If the above is true, then when \(\Psi\) is unknown, by Slutsky theorem, \(C_{1-\alpha} = \{ \rho:  \ n(\hat{\rho} - \rho)^T\hat\Psi(\hat\rho)^{-1}(\hat{\rho} - \rho)\ \leq \chi^{2}_{d, 1-\alpha} \}\)
I do think the confidence ellipsoid should be the intersect of \(C_{1-\alpha}\) and the PSD criteria.



Practical Considerations:

When \(\Psi(\rho)\) is unknown, we can try its plug-in estimate: \(\Psi(\hat{\rho})\). This requires consistency check.
We also want to check that the Wald pivot statistic using plug-in \(\Psi(\hat{\rho})\) has the correct \(\chi^2\) calibration. - See Simulation 4 (Reverse Containment Rate) for empirical check.
\[
T^* = \ n(\hat\rho - \rho_0)^T \Psi(\hat\rho)^{-1}(\hat\rho-\rho_0)
\]
If Wald-approximation is correct using the plug-in approach, then \(P(T^* \leq \chi^2_{d, 1-\alpha}) \approx 1- \alpha\)

text:
Simulation 1: Nominal vs Actual Coverage
Goal is to validate:
\[
Pr_\rho(\rho \in C_{1-\alpha}(\hat\rho)) = 1-\alpha
\]
Frequentist interpretation of confidence region: Over repeated samples, the confidence region (which is random, depends on sample) contains the fixed true \(\rho\) with probability \(1-\alpha\).

Simulation Flow: Monte Carlo estimate of coverage of \(C_{1-\alpha}(\hat{\rho})\)
Input: \(\rho_0\), \(\Psi(\rho_0)\), sample size \(n\), significance level \(\alpha\), number of replicates \(B\)
Output: Coverage level \(C_{1-\alpha}(\hat\rho)\)
\(H \leftarrow 0\)
for \(b\) \(\leftarrow\) 1 to \(B\):

Sample \(\hat\rho^{(b)}\) from Wald-cloud (or equivalently, normal distribution)
Compute covariance \(\hat\Psi(\hat\rho^{(b)})\)
Compute mahalanobis distance \(T_b \leftarrow n(\hat{\rho}^{(b)}-\rho_{0})^{\top}[\hat\Psi(\rho_{0})]^{-1}(\hat{\rho}^{(b)}-\rho_{0})\)
if \(T_b \leq \chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}\), then \(H \leftarrow H+1\) ;

return \(H /B\) (actual coverage)

This simulation repeats over different \(\rho_0\)’s sampled from the rlkj distribution under different \(\eta\). Sample size \(n\) is set to \(1e6\) to mirror aysmptotic-ness, \(\alpha = 0.05, 0.10\), \(B=  200\), and repeated over 50 different \(\rho_0\).

title: 3D Correlation Space
text:
Generating random samples around \(\rho_0\)
What are the different approach to generate random samples?

Generate MVN data based on \(\hat\rho\) and compute its correlation vector \(\hat\rho^{\prime}\)
Generate \(\hat\rho^{\prime}\) from \(\hat\rho\) directly: sample randomly from the full distributional spread around \(\rho_0\) (wald-cloud).


Sample from full distribution of \(\rho_0\)
Let \(\rho_0 = vech(R_0)\). For testing \(H_0: \rho = \rho_0\), based on asymptotic normality of \(\hat\rho\), we have wald-type statistic (same as previously mentioned)
\[
T = n (\hat\rho - \rho_0)^T \Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\hat\rho - \rho_0) \sim \chi^2_p
\]
This implies we can draw \(\hat\rho\) under the null distribution \(H_0\):
\[
\hat\rho^{(b)} \sim N_p(\rho_0, \frac{\Psi(\rho_0)}{n})
\]
Equivalently, the linear algebra approach:
\(\hat\rho^{(b)} = \rho_0 + Lz\), where \(z \sim N(0,I_p)\), \(L= \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}UD^\frac{1}{2}\) (eigen-decomposition of \(\Psi(\rho_0)\): \(U\) is the eigenvectors , \(D\) is the eigenvalue matrix)
This should give us below statement when \(n\) is infinite, \[
Pr_{\rho_0} (\rho \in C_{1-\alpha}(\hat\rho)) = 1-\alpha
\]


Uniform samples inside the confidence region of \(\rho_0\)
The goal is to generate uniform and random samples within \(C_{1-\alpha}(\rho_0)\) with guarantee: \(C_{1-\alpha} = \{ \rho:  \ n(\hat{\rho} - \rho_0)^T\Psi^{-1}(\hat{\rho} - \rho_0)\ \leq \chi^{2}_{p, 1-\alpha} \}\)
Modifying from the wald-cloud approach (matrix notation), a random uniform sample can be constructed by:
\[
\hat\rho^{(b)} = \rho_0 + L(\sqrt{c} r^{\frac{1}{p}}Z)
\]
where \(c: \chi^2_{p, 1-\alpha}\), \(r\) represent a random radius sample from \(Unif(0,1)\), \(Z\) represents the random unit direction, sample from \(N(0,I_p)\) and rescale to have length (norm) 1 (i.e. \(||Z|| = 1\))
My intuition on this:
\(c\) sets the \(1-\alpha\) chi-square cut-off that determines the confidence ellipsoid boundary; \(r\) distributes a random radius (between (0,1)) uniformly in all \(p\)-dimension within the ellipsoid; \(Z\) is the standard way to generate uniform random directions on a unit sphere. Geometrically, multiplying these three objects to \(L\)is like rotating and scaling the ellipsoid.
Notes:

We are limiting the samples within \(C_{1-\alpha}\) as well they have equal “weights” (hence uniform), the Mahalanobis distance is no longer a valid chi-square statistic. (Is this important to further deep-dive? Use the resulting distribution to calibrate more easily if the distribution is in simple closed form?)
To be more exact, the uniformity refers to the ratio of the sample ellipsoid volume to the CI ellipsoid’s volume. Proof:
Given any point \(\rho\), we have
\[
E(c) = \{ \rho : n(\rho - \rho_0)^T \Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\rho - \rho_0) \leq c \}
\]
where \(c=\chi^2_{p, 1-\alpha}\)
Now suppose we have a random \(\rho\) from \(\rho_0\) that is measured by a distance \(t\), we have:
\[
\rho(t) = \rho_0+ \sqrt{\frac{t}{c}} (\rho - \rho_0)
\] Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\rho(t) - \rho_0)^T\Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\rho(t) - \rho_0)
&= (\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}} (\rho - \rho_0))^T\Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}} (\rho - \rho_0)) \\  
&=
\frac{t}{c} (\rho - \rho_0))^T\Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\rho - \rho_0)) \\&= \frac{t}{c} \frac{c}{n} \\ &= \frac{t}{n}
\end{aligned}
\] Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{V(E(\rho(t))}{V(E(c))} &= \frac{V(\rho_0+ \sqrt{\frac{t}{c}} (\rho - \rho_0))}{V(E(c))} \\ &= \frac{(\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}})^p \cdot V(\rho))}{V(E(c))} \\ &= \frac{(\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}})^p \cdot V(E(c)))}{V(E(c))} \\ &= (\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}})^p \\ &= (\frac{t}{c})^{(p/2)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Note: The distance \(t\) is exactly the mahalanobis distance of a sample to \(\rho_0\). This ratio should be approximately \(Unif(0,1)\).
[Attach Example]



Visualization of random uniform samples










Why don’t we use the first approach (generate data then compute correlation) ?

Making extra assumption: This approach assumes the underlying data distribution, which seems to be unnecessary here in our theory. We only need \(\hat\rho\) to be normal (asymptotically).
To meet out goal as a less expensive approach for resampling. Sample from \(\rho\) directly will be a less expensive approach.

Notes:

Previously discuss a sphere-cloud approach, I modified it to the “wald-cloud” (approach 2) above, this is to consider the covariance of correlation under null.
The rank deficient problem and implications:

Given a \(\rho_0\), if \(\Psi(\rho_0)\) is rank-deficient, the above approach will not be feasible. Either choose a different \(\rho_0\) , or use a different approach to conduct inference.
A few approaches we discussed so far:

Z-transformation on \(\rho\) to stabilize variance. (not included yet)
Only work within the rank-reduced space; the “null-space” will be treated as “constraints”. In this case, degree of freedom will be reduced. Also, is it still chi-square?

text:
Simulation 1: Empirical distribution of the observed test statistic (mahalanobis distance/ wald).
Goal: To assess whether the empirical distribution of the simulated Wald test statistic matches the theoretical \(\chi^2\) density under \(H_0\)​, which validates the chi-square calibration of the procedure, including Type-1 error and coverage.

Simulation Flow:
Input: True R \(\rho_0\), sample size \(n\), significance level \(\alpha\), number of replicates \(B\)
Output: Test statistic (mahalanobis distance) \(T_b\)
for \(b\) \(\leftarrow\) 1 to \(B\):

Sample \(\hat\rho^{(b)}\) from Wald-cloud (or equivalently, normal distribution)
Compute covariance \(\Psi(\hat\rho^{(b)})\)
Compute test-statistic (mahalanobis distance): \(T_b \leftarrow n(\hat{\rho}^{(b)}-\rho_{0})^{\top}[\Psi(\rho_{0})]^{-1}(\hat{\rho}^{(b)}-\rho_{0})\)

return \(T_b\)

Note: When true variance is known, use \(\Psi(\rho_0)\). When true variance is unknown, \(\Psi(\hat\rho^{(b)})\) can be a good estimate of
The histogram shows the empirical distribution of the observed test statistics \(T_b\) from simulation, the red curve shows the theoretical \(\chi^2\) density under \(H_0\)​.

title: 3D Correlation Space
text:
Simulation 2: Nominal vs Actual Coverage
Goal is to validate:
\[
Pr_\rho(\rho \in C_{1-\alpha}(\hat\rho)) = 1-\alpha
\]
Frequentist interpretation of confidence region: Over repeated samples, the confidence region (which is random, depends on sample) contains the fixed true \(\rho\) with probability \(1-\alpha\).

Simulation Flow: Monte Carlo estimate of coverage of \(C_{1-\alpha}(\hat{\rho})\)
Input: \(\rho_0\), \(\Psi(\rho_0)\), sample size \(n\), significance level \(\alpha\), number of replicates \(B\)
Output: Coverage level \(C_{1-\alpha}(\hat\rho)\)
\(H \leftarrow 0\)
for \(b\) \(\leftarrow\) 1 to \(B\):

Sample \(\hat\rho^{(b)}\) from Wald-cloud (or equivalently, normal distribution)
Compute covariance \(\hat\Psi(\hat\rho^{(b)})\)
Compute test-statistic (mahalanobis distance): \(T_b \leftarrow n(\hat{\rho}^{(b)}-\rho_{0})^{\top}[\hat\Psi(\rho_{0})]^{-1}(\hat{\rho}^{(b)}-\rho_{0})\)
if \(T_b \leq \chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}\), then \(H \leftarrow H+1\) ;

return \(H /B\) (actual coverage)


Output
For each \(\rho_0\) (sample from a fixed \(\eta\)), I generated \(B=300\) perturbed samples and evaluate the actual coverage under nominal levels \(\alpha \in {0.05, 0.10}\). Sample size \(n\) is fixed at 1e6 to approximate the asymptotic assumption. For each \(\eta\), \(G\)=50 \(\rho_0\)s were sampled.
countNA: if a \(\Psi(\rho_0)\) is rank-deficient, that means the existing approach does not allow us to sample under the null distribution, therefore we skip this \(\rho_0\) sample. When \(\eta=0.1\), samples are close to the boundary, and more than half of them have rank-deficient covariance. However, when it is not rank-deficient, the coverage behaves normal.

title: 3D Correlation Space
text:
Marginal inference approach

We discussed instead of the joint-inference approach, we could sample \(\hat\rho_{ij}\) independently from its asymptotic distribution \(N(\rho_{ij}, 1-\rho_{ij}^2)\).

From simulation (similar to simulation 2 above), coverage of each \(\hat\rho_{ij}\) is close to the nominal level when considered individually. However, when we consider the results across all \(\rho_{ij}\) s jointly, the joint coverage from this marginal approach became poor. This is related to multiple testing problem.
To construct a correlation matrix sample, we could sample each \(\hat\rho_{ij}\) independently from its confidence interval, and check if that constructed matrix is PSD. If it is not PSD, we reject it.
This approach works in lower dimension, however became highly inefficient (large rejection rate) as dimension grows.

title: 3D Correlation Space
text:
Sampling

Sampling distribution of \(\hat\rho\): Multivariate normal distribution (Full Wald Cloud)
We introduced that the asymptotic distribution of \(\hat\rho\) is the following:
\[
\sqrt{n}(\hat{\rho}-\rho) \xrightarrow{d} N_d(0,\Psi(\rho))
\]
which is equivalent to \(\hat\rho \sim N_d(\rho, \frac{\Psi(\rho)}{n})\) after rearranging the terms. In other words, if we know \(\rho\) and \(\Psi(\rho)\), we can obtain random \(\hat\rho\) samples following the above MVN distribution. Importantly, these samples respect the covariance of \(\rho\).
In matrix algebra notation:
\(\hat\rho = \rho + Lz\), where \(z \sim N(0,I_p)\), \(L= \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}UD^\frac{1}{2}\) (eigen-decomposition of \(\Psi(\rho)\): \(U\) is the eigenvector, \(D\) is the eigenvalue matrix).
Interpretation: Suppose we draw 100 \(\hat\rho\)s from the sampling distribution, approximately 95 \(\hat\rho\)s will satisfy the Mahalanobis inequality, which implies that approximately 95 out of the 100 confidence regions constructed by each \(\hat\rho\)s will contain the true parameter \(\rho\):
\[
Pr_{\rho_0} (\rho \in C_{1-\alpha}(\hat\rho)) = 1-\alpha
\]
See also:

Simulation 1



Sample inside the confidence region of \(\rho\)
To achieve this, we will have to determine: (1) the boundary of \(\rho\), (2) Sampling scheme inside the boundary space (e.g., do we sample uniformly or normally?).

1. Boundary of \(\rho\)
Suppose we want to know the boundary of 95% confidence region of \(\rho\), and suppose this \(\rho\) is fixed at \(\rho_0\). The maximum mahalanobis distance is \(c= \chi^2_{d,0.95}\).
Following the matrix algebra notation in earlier section, the boundary is determined at \(\hat\rho^b = \rho_0 + L\sqrt{c}\) (Note: superscript \(b\) denotes boundary).


2. Sampling Scheme

A truncated wald cloud approach: Sample from the full wald cloud, and reject samples that failed the inequality test. Caveat: we might lose 5% of samples.
Sample normally inside the boundary:
Note that the boundary is \(\rho_0 + L\sqrt{c}\). Normally distributed samples inside this region can be generated by
\[
\hat\rho^{(b)} = \rho_0 + L(\sqrt{q} Z)
\]
where \(L= \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}UD^\frac{1}{2}\) (eigen-decomposition of \(\Psi(\rho)\): \(U\) is the eigenvector, \(D\) is the eigenvalue matrix), \(q\) is a random sample from \(\chi^2_{d, 0.95}\), and \(Z\) represents random unit direction on each dimension, sample from \(N(0,I_p)\) and rescale to norm of 1 (i.e. \(||Z|| = 1\))
Sample uniformly inside the boundary:
\[
\hat\rho^{(b)} = \rho_0 + L(\sqrt{c} r^{\frac{1}{p}}Z)
\]
where \(c: \chi^2_{d, 1-\alpha}\), \(r\) represent a random radius sample from \(Unif(0,1)\), \(Z\) represents random unit direction on each dimension, sample from \(N(0,I_p)\) and rescale to norm of 1 (i.e. \(||Z|| = 1\)).

If the boundary is defined as \(C_{1-\alpha}\), then all resulting samples above (regardless of sampling scheme) will guarantee to fall inside \(C_{1-\alpha}\),
Interpretation:
\(c\) sets the \(1-\alpha\) chi-square cut-off that determines the confidence ellipsoid boundary; \(r\) distributes a random radius (between (0,1)) uniformly in all \(p\)-dimension within the ellipsoid; \(Z\) is the standard way to generate uniform random directions on a unit sphere. Geometrically, multiplying these three objects to \(L\)is like rotating and scaling the ellipsoid.



Practical considerations
All sampling approaches require \(\rho\) to have a well-defined covariance \(\Psi(\rho)\). If \(\Psi\) is rank-deficient, we will not be able to proceed with the sampling procedure above. Some ideas to work in later stage:

Z-transformation on \(\rho\) could potentially help to stabilize variance. (not implemented yet)
Only work within the rank-reduced space; the “null-space” will be treated as “constraints”: make pertubations using a subset of those stable dimensions / variables. In this case, degree of freedom will be reduced. Also, is it still chi-square?

Notes:

Mahalanobis distance is no longer a valid chi-square statistic (distribution) if we are limiting samples within \(C_{1-\alpha}\) and changing the normal density to uniform. (Is this important to further deep-dive? Use the resulting distribution to calibrate more easily if the distribution is in simple closed form?)
[Jon: review below again] To be more precise on the uniform sampling scheme, the uniformity refers to the ratio of the sample ellipsoid volume to the CI ellipsoid’s volume is uniform. Proof:
Given any point \(\rho\), we have
\[
E(c) = \{ \rho : n(\rho - \rho_0)^T \Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\rho - \rho_0) \leq c \}
\]
where \(c=\chi^2_{p, 1-\alpha}\)
Now suppose we have a random \(\rho\) that is \(t\) distant away from \(\rho_0\) in the Mahalanobis space:
\[
\rho= \rho_0+ \sqrt{\frac{t}{c}} (\rho - \rho_0)
\] Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\rho(t) - \rho_0)^T\Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\rho(t) - \rho_0)
&= (\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}} (\rho - \rho_0))^T\Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}} (\rho - \rho_0)) \\  
&=
\frac{t}{c} (\rho - \rho_0))^T\Psi(\rho_0)^{-1} (\rho - \rho_0)) \\&= \frac{t}{c} \frac{c}{n} \\ &= \frac{t}{n}
\end{aligned}
\] Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{V(E(\rho(t))}{V(E(c))} &= \frac{V(\rho_0+ \sqrt{\frac{t}{c}} (\rho - \rho_0))}{V(E(c))} \\ &= \frac{(\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}})^p \cdot V(\rho))}{V(E(c))} \\ &= \frac{(\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}})^p \cdot V(E(c)))}{V(E(c))} \\ &= (\sqrt{\frac{t}{c}})^p \\ &= (\frac{t}{c})^{(p/2)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Note: The distance \(t\) is exactly the mahalanobis distance of a sample to \(\rho_0\). This ratio should be approximately \(Unif(0,1)\).

Simulation 5: MCMC Sampling
Setup: Start with a graph \(G\) that is parametrized by \(R_0\). We observed data \(X\) with sample size \(n\) and derive sample correlation \(S\).
Procedure:

Initialize a chain \(Q\) with \(S\): \(Q^{[0]} = S\)
From \(t=1, .... , B\):
Let \(R\) denote current state: \(Q^{[t]}\)

Sample \(R' \sim W(R;\Psi(R, n))\)
Compute acceptance ratio: \(A(R \rightarrow R') = \dfrac{f(R | R',n)}{f(R'|R,n)}\cdot\ I(S \in CR_{1-\alpha}(R') )\)

\(f(R| R',n)\) is the multivariate normal density of \(R\) given \(\mu = R'\) and \(\Sigma = \Psi(R')/n\)
\(I(S \in CR_{1-\alpha}(R') )\) is an indicator function for the reverse containment status. \(I(\cdot)=1\) if \(S\) lies within the confidence region of \(R'\) at level \(1-\alpha\). The center is \(R'\).
More specifically, it is checking the Mahalanobis distance between \(S\) and \(R'\) with \(R'\) as the center: \((s−r′)^T \Psi(R′)^{-1}(s−r′)≤\chi^2_{d,1−α}​\), where \(d=\frac{p(p-1)}{2}\).

If \(A(R→R′) >u\) where \(u \sim Unif(0,1)\), accept \(R'\): update \(Q^{[t]} = R'\). Else, \(Q^{[t]} = Q^{[t-1]} = R\)


Other notes: Burnin period was set as 20% of samples in the chain.
